blocks.heading: A Harness for Every Task
blocks.text: A Harness for Every Task Part 13 announced dynamic workflows at launch. A week later, Thariq Shihipar and Sid Bidasaria - the engineers who built the feature - published the practitioner's guide: how workflows actually work, the patterns Claude composes, and where they pay off (often on non-coding work). "Claude can now write its own harness on the fly, custom-built for the task at hand." This is the how-to behind the launch note. Best practices are still developing, and workflows often use more tokens - so think about when to reach for one. @trq212 + @sidbid's article · June 2026 Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: Why Workflows - Three Failure Modes They Fix
blocks.text: 1 Why Workflows - Three Failure Modes They Fix The default Claude Code harness plans and executes in one context window. For most coding tasks that's highly effective. It breaks down on the long-running, massively parallel, or adversarial tasks - and the longer Claude works in a single window, the more three specific failure modes creep in. Agentic laziness Claude stops before finishing a complex, multi-part task and declares it done after partial progress - addressing 20 of the 50 items in a security review and calling it complete. Self-preferential bias Claude tends to prefer its own results, especially when asked to verify or judge its work against a rubric. The grader and the author being the same context is the problem. Goal drift Gradual loss of fidelity to the original objective across many turns - worst after compaction. Each summarization step is lossy, and details like edge-case requirements or "don't do X" constraints quietly fall out. The fix A workflow orchestrates separate Claudes, each with its own context window and a focused, isolated goal . Laziness loses to a deterministic loop that doesn't exit until every item is handled; bias loses to a different agent doing the judging; drift loses because each agent holds one small goal that never gets summarized away. This connects straight to Part 13's honesty story - a model that overclaims at step 4 wastes the next 40 steps. ← intro primitives →

blocks.heading: The Primitives - and Dynamic vs Static
blocks.text: 2 The Primitives - and Dynamic vs Static A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript file with a few special functions that spawn and coordinate subagents. Standard JSON , Math , and Array are there too for processing data. # spawn one subagent - schema forces validated JSON back const bugs = await agent("audit auth.ts", { schema: BugList, // JSON Schema → validated output model: "haiku", // opus · sonnet · haiku · omit = inherit isolation: "worktree", // own checkout, for parallel edits agentType: "reviewer", // custom / built-in subagent }) Compose the block parallel([ fns ]) - fan out, run at once. A barrier : it waits for all of them, then you have every result together. pipeline(items, ...stages) - each item streams through every stage independently. No barrier : item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. Claude decides which model each agent uses and whether it runs in its own worktree - picking the intelligence level and isolation the step actually needs. Resumable by default Interrupt a workflow - quit the terminal, cancel mid-run - and resuming the session picks up where it left off. The deterministic harness remembers what already completed. Dynamic vs static You may have built static workflows before with the Agent SDK or claude -p . Because a static workflow has to handle every edge case, it ends up generic: "turn this into 5 web searches → fetch → verify → summarize → a generic report." With Opus 4.8, Claude is smart enough to write a custom harness tailor-made for your case : "read our billing code → check each feature against the new provider's docs → devil's advocate the strongest case against migrating → a specific recommendation." ← why workflows six patterns →

blocks.heading: The Six Patterns Claude Composes
blocks.text: 3 The Six Patterns Claude Composes Building a mental model for these helps you nudge Claude via prompts. They're not exclusive - Claude mixes and nests them. 1 · Classify-and-act A classifier agent decides the type of task, then routes to different agents or behavior. Or classify at the end to shape the output. 2 · Fan-out-and-synthesize Split into many smaller steps, run an agent on each, then synthesize. The synthesize step is a barrier - it waits for all the fan-out agents, then merges their structured outputs into one result. Best when each step benefits from its own clean context so they don't cross-contaminate. 3 · Adversarial verification For each spawned agent, run a separate agent to adversarially verify its output against a rubric. The verifier is never the author - that's what kills self-preferential bias. 4 · Generate-and-filter Generate many ideas on a topic, then filter by a rubric or by verification, dedupe, and return only the highest-quality, tested few. 5 · Tournament Instead of dividing work, have agents compete . Spawn N agents that each attempt the same task a different way, then judge them pairwise until you have a winner. Comparative judgment is more reliable than absolute scoring. 6 · Loop-until-done For an unknown amount of work, keep spawning agents until a stop condition is met - no new findings, no more errors in the logs - instead of a fixed number of passes. Simple counters miss the tail. ← primitives use cases →

blocks.heading: Use Cases - Often Better for Non-Coding Work
blocks.text: 4 Use Cases - Often Better for Non-Coding Work Thariq: "I've found that workflows are sometimes even more useful for non-technical work." A sampling from the article: Migrations & refactors Bun was rewritten from Zig to Rust using workflows. Break the task into units - callsites, failing tests, modules - spin off a subagent for each fix in its own worktree, have another agent adversarially review, then merge. Tell agents to avoid resource-intensive commands so you can maximally parallelize without melting your machine. Deep research & deep verification The /deep-research skill is itself a workflow: fan out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify their claims, synthesize a cited report. The inverse is deep verification - one agent extracts every factual claim from a report, a subagent checks each in detail, and an optional source-auditor agent confirms the source is high quality. "Verify every technical claim in my blog draft against the codebase - I don't want to ship anything wrong." Sorting 1,000+ items You can't sort 1,000 rows by a qualitative measure in one prompt - quality degrades and it won't fit in context. Run a tournament , a pipeline of pairwise-comparison agents (comparative judgment beats absolute scoring), or bucket-rank in parallel then merge. Each comparison is its own agent; the deterministic loop holds the bracket so only the running order stays in context. Memory & rule adherence For rules Claude keeps missing even in CLAUDE.md: one verifier agent per rule , plus a skeptic persona that reviews the rules to avoid false positives. The reverse direction works too - mine your recent sessions and code-review comments for corrections you keep making, cluster them, adversarially verify each candidate ("would this rule have prevented a real mistake?"), and distill the survivors back into CLAUDE.md. Root-cause investigation Debugging works best with several independent hypotheses tested in parallel - but one context window invites self-preferential bias. A workflow spins up agents that generate hypotheses from disjoint evidence (logs, files, data), then each hypothesis faces a panel of verifiers and refuters. Works for sales ("why did sales drop in March?"), data engineering, any post-mortem. Triage, taste, evals, routing Triage at scale: classify each backlog item, dedupe against what's already tracked, then fix or escalate. Use a quarantine pattern - agents reading untrusted public content can't take high-privilege actions. Pair with /loop to run continuously. Exploration & taste: for design or naming, give a review agent a rubric; the task is done when the rubric is met. Order options via tournament. Evals: spin agents in worktrees, then comparison agents grade outputs against a rubric - handy for refining a skill you're building. Model routing: a classifier researches the task, then routes to Sonnet or Opus based on expected complexity. ← six patterns loop + budgets →

blocks.heading: Pair With /goal, /loop, and Token Budgets
blocks.text: 5 Pair With /goal, /loop, and Token Budgets Workflows compose with the rest of Claude Code. Three levers worth knowing, plus the honest "when not to." /goal + /loop For repeatable workflows - triage, research, verification - pair with /loop to run at regular intervals and /goal to set a hard completion requirement. This is the Part 12 + Part 13 arc closing: /goal sets the exit condition, the workflow does the parallel work, /loop keeps it going. Token budgets Workflows are token-hungry, so cap them. Prompt a budget directly - "use 10k tokens" - and the workflow holds the ceiling. $ Use a workflow to rank these 80 resumes for the backend role and double-check the top ten. use 50k tokens See what's burning tokens: /usage When a long autonomous run eats your limits faster than expected, run /usage for a breakdown of the specific skills, MCPs, and plugins spending your tokens. Boris points people here first when they hit limits mid-run - it's how you find the workflow or MCP that's quietly dominating the bill. Quick workflows They aren't only for big jobs. Prompt a "quick workflow" for something small - a fast adversarial review of a single assumption, for instance. When not to use one Workflows can use significantly more tokens and aren't needed for every task. Thariq: "For regular coding tasks, ask yourself: does it really need more compute? Most traditional coding tasks do not need a panel of 5 reviewers." Use them to push Claude in ways you couldn't before - not as the default for a 20-line change. ← use cases save + share →

blocks.heading: Save and Share Your Workflows
blocks.text: 6 Save and Share Your Workflows A good workflow is reusable. Once Claude builds one you like, keep it. Save it Press "s" in the workflow menu to save. Check the files into ~/.claude/workflows , or distribute them via a skill. Dynamic workflows 1 running · 2 completed ⟩ ✓ review-changes · 14 agents · 482k tok · 6m 12s ◴ find-flaky-tests · 6 agents · 121k tok · 1m 48s ✓ deep-research · 22 agents · 1.1M tok · 11m 3s ↑/↓ select · enter view · s save · esc close Share via a skill Put your JavaScript workflow files in the skill folder and reference them in the SKILL.md . For flexibility, prompt Claude to treat the workflows in a skill as a template , not a script to run verbatim - so it adapts the harness to the specific case instead of replaying it blindly. The "ultracode" trigger You can start a workflow just by asking for one - or use the trigger word "ultracode" to guarantee Claude Code builds a workflow rather than running a single pass. This is the fourth pillar settling into place: Part 11's auto mode, Part 12's agent view + /goal , Part 13's Opus 4.8 + the workflow launch, and now the patterns to drive them. Thariq's closing line is the honest one - "there's still much to discover in how to use them best." Research preview. Best practices are still developing. ← loop + budgets back to intro →

blocks.heading: Reflecting on a Year of Claude Code
blocks.text: Reflecting on a Year of Claude Code One year after Claude Code went GA, Boris Cherny (Head of Claude Code) and Cat Wu (Head of Product) sat down to talk about what changed - "from a Slack demo that got two reactions to engineering teams deploying it across entire codebases." Four ideas stood out, and a couple quietly overturned earlier advice on this very site: why Boris dropped plan mode, the shift to context minimalism, the one habit that lets Claude run for hours, and why auto mode is safer than reading every prompt. @bcherny + @_catwu · June 8, 2026 Watch: "Reflecting on a year of Claude Code" Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: Auto Mode Retired Plan Mode (Opus 4.6+)
blocks.text: 1 Auto Mode Retired Plan Mode (Opus 4.6+) For over a year, plan mode was Boris's go-to for synchronous coding. A year after GA, he's moved on - and the reason is the model, not the feature. In his words "What it used to be is plan mode. I don't use that anymore. I use auto mode - instead of plan mode. The newer models don't actually need a planning step. It was really important for Opus 4 through 4.5, but starting with 4.6, and definitely with 4.7, it just doesn't need it." Why it changed Older models needed an explicit plan to stay on track. 4.6+ plan implicitly, so the planning step became overhead - an artifact to review before any work starts. What he does instead Start Claude in auto mode, let it work, move to the next Claude. No babysitting. Some people keep plan mode for the written artifact, and that's fine - Boris just runs auto mode for everything. Updates Part 1 This revises the plan-mode tip from Part 1. The rule of thumb shifted with the model: pre-4.6, plan first; 4.6 and later, let it run. Pairs with the auto mode tips in Parts 8 and 11. ← intro minimalism →

blocks.heading: Context Minimalism - Tell the Model Less
blocks.text: 2 Context Minimalism - Tell the Model Less "From context engineering to context minimalism" is its own chapter in the interview. The era you're in tracks the model you're using. The progression Sonnet 3.5 was the era of prompt engineering . Opus 4 was the era of context engineering . Today's models need neither. Boris "You give it the minimal possible system prompt, the minimal possible tools, and then you let the model figure it out. You just have to give the model some way to pull in the context." Cat "I'm a context minimalist. Tell the model only what it needs to know and let it figure out the rest. When you give the model too much context, it's like you're micromanaging it - and sometimes the model knows a better way to get to the same outcome." The move Stop front-loading giant prompts and tool lists. Give a lean brief plus a way to fetch context - files, search, MCP - then get out of the way. Minimal ≠ vague: give the goal, not the micro-steps. Pairs with Part 10's "delegation over guidance." ← plan → auto write it down →

blocks.heading: When Claude Errs, Write It Down - Don't Re-Prompt
blocks.text: 3 When Claude Errs, Write It Down - Don't Re-Prompt Boris calls this the single most important idea for long-running work - and it's the whole reason his agents can run for hours. In his words "Every single time Claude makes a mistake, I don't tell it to do it differently. I tell it to write it to the CLAUDE.md, or make a skill, or something. If you can do this, then Claude can just run forever." The distinction Correcting Claude in chat fixes this one run . Writing the fix into CLAUDE.md or a skill fixes every future run . A conversational correction is a patch; a written rule is a fix. Why it compounds The error rate trends down over time instead of resetting each session. The rule set grows; the mistakes don't come back. When something goes wrong, your next instruction isn't "do it this way" - it's "add a rule so this doesn't happen again." Pairs with Part 1's CLAUDE.md and Skills tips, and Part 10's /rewind over correcting. ← minimalism auto mode safety →

blocks.heading: Why Auto Mode Is Trustworthy - Red-Teaming and Evals
blocks.text: 4 Why Auto Mode Is Trustworthy - Red-Teaming and Evals Auto mode routes each action to a classifier instead of asking you to approve every prompt. The interview explains why you can trust it - and why it's arguably safer than reading every prompt yourself. How it was hardened The team collected thousands of full agent transcripts plus the permission prompt, had auto mode classify each as safe or unsafe, then brought in red-teamers to prompt-inject and attack the codebase. Those attacks became evals ; auto mode was tuned until it caught them all. The counterintuitive part "When you accept 99% of requests, your eyes glaze over. Auto mode is more safe than reading every single permission prompt because it means you're only paying attention to the most important thing." The payoff Because he trusts it, he can let one agent run and start a second. Trust is what makes parallel, autonomous work possible - it protects against today's known vulnerabilities and the most intelligent attacks the team can construct. Pairs with the auto mode tips in Parts 8 and 11. ← write it down back to intro →

blocks.heading: Nested Subagents - Agents Kicking Off Agents
blocks.text: 1 Nested Subagents - Agents Kicking Off Agents Boris: "Just landed nested subagent support in Claude Code. Starting to experiment more with agents kicking off agents as a way to better manage context. Capped at depth=5 to start." What it is A subagent can now spawn its own subagents, down to depth=5 (a starting cap). Nesting is a context-management tool - each layer keeps its own context window, so deep work doesn't bloat the parent. Monitor them To watch what each subagent is doing, hit arrow-down in the terminal. (Asked how to see them, Boris: "In terminal? Hit arrow down." ) Model propagates, thinking weights don't (yet) Dispatched subagents can run on a chosen model; per a user's testing that Boris confirmed, the model carries through but thinking weights do not propagate yet. Nesting also works with forked sessions and subagents can use Chrome . Where a dynamic workflow (Parts 13-14) is an orchestrated harness, nested subagents are the lower-level primitive - any agent can delegate to keep its own context clean. Pairs with Part 1's subagents + worktrees and Part 12's agent view. ← intro fork: true →

blocks.heading: fork: true - Run a Skill in Its Own Context Window
blocks.text: 2 fork: true - Run a Skill in Its Own Context Window An idea Boris shared in the same thread, framed explicitly as "one idea I'm experimenting with" - so treat it as a preview, not a stable API. The mechanic Add fork: true to a skill's frontmatter so the skill runs in its own context window , then have the skill use agents to keep context isolated per step. --- skill frontmatter --- name: my-skill fork: true In his words "add 'fork:true' to a skill's frontmatter to have it run in its own context window, then in the skill tell it to use agents to keep context isolated for each step also. Adding this to the built in /code-review skill to improve performance even more." Why A heavy skill (deep research, code review) can pollute or blow out the main context. Forking gives it a clean window; per-step agents (tip 1) isolate further. Same instinct as Part 15's context minimalism - keep each unit of work to the smallest context it needs. ← nested agents use a workflow →

blocks.heading: The Dynamic-Workflows Trigger Is Now "use a workflow"
blocks.text: 3 The Dynamic-Workflows Trigger Is Now "use a workflow" A correction to the activation trigger from Part 13 and Part 14. The launch said the bare word "workflow" in a prompt was the trigger. Boris has refined it: In his words "Say 'use a workflow'. Just 'workflow' had too many false positives." Do this To launch a dynamic workflow, say "use a workflow" - e.g. "use a workflow to rank these 80 resumes" - not just the word "workflow." Updates Parts 13 & 14 The workflow mechanics in Parts 13-14 are unchanged - orchestrator → implementer → verifiers → fixer, hundreds of agents, default to auto mode. Only the trigger phrasing tightened. ← fork: true back to intro →

blocks.heading: Fable 5 - The Launch
blocks.text: 1 Fable 5 - The Launch The announcement from Claude: "Introducing Claude Fable 5: a Mythos-class model that we've made safe for general use. Its capabilities exceed those of any model we've ever made generally available." Available now in Claude Code and Cowork . Boris's verdict "Fable is the best model I have used for coding, by a wide margin. It is a big step up, enabling less prompts and steers, more efficient token use, better code quality, better tool use, more intelligent self-verification, longer running sessions, and higher trust & autonomy." "Big model smell" - Boris on living with it "With Fable, it's felt like Claude has stepped up from being a coding agent to a thought and design partner... Fable has judgement, taste, and dimensionality in a way that previous models didn't. The first time I had this realization was when I asked Fable to debug something - it's the first model I've used that was so methodical and precise, taking measurements and adding logs then verifying that it truly fixed the issue before declaring victory. There's nothing in Claude Code's prompting telling it to do that; it's just part of its personality. It really has this 'big model smell.'" That self-verifying debugging is the Verification (Part 1) + Opus 4.8 honesty (Part 13) thread paying off in the base model. Boris on living with Fable 5 The step-ups, at a glance Fewer prompts & steers More efficient token use Better code quality & tool use More intelligent self-verification Longer-running sessions Higher trust & autonomy The benchmarks (Fable 5 → Opus 4.8 → GPT 5.5 → Gemini 3.1 Pro) Claude: "state-of-the-art on nearly all tested benchmarks... the longer and more complex the task, the larger Fable 5's lead." Agentic coding, SWE-Bench Pro: 80.3% → 69.2 → 58.6 → 54.2 Frontier coding, FrontierCode/Diamond (xhigh): 29.3% → 13.4 → 5.7 → - Knowledge work, GDPval-AA: 1932 → 1890 → 1769 → 1314 Spatial reasoning, Blueprint-Bench 2: 38.6% → 14.5 → 36.2 → 26.5 Computer use, OSWorld-Verified: 85.0% → 83.4 → 78.7 → 76.2 Accuracy note: "Fable 5" is the Mythos-class model made safe for general use; the table reports the higher of Mythos 5 / Fable 5 (within 1-3 pts). On the starred benchmarks (cybersecurity, biology, Terminal-Bench, Humanity's Last Exam, HealthBench), Fable 5 performs closer to Opus 4.8 due to safety fallbacks - so treat those higher figures as Mythos 5. Boris confirms the classifiers are currently "trigger-happy" (flagging ordinary debugging as cyber/bio) and the team is "working on improving it." A second voice - Andrej Karpathy (now at Anthropic) "It's SOTA on everything by a margin... qualitatively, a major-version-bump-deserving step change forward. You can give it a lot more ambitious tasks than what you're used to - the model 'gets it' and it will just go. It's never felt this tempting to stop looking at the code at all (but don't do this in prod!)." He adds the safeguards are "a little too trigger-happy for launch" - the same fallbacks behind the starred benchmarks above. Karpathy's take ← intro what changes →

blocks.heading: What Fable 5 Changes for You
blocks.text: 2 What Fable 5 Changes for You Fable 5 supersedes Opus 4.8 as the strongest coding model - which shifts a couple of earlier tips and leans harder into others. It's the new default for coding Updates Part 1's "use Opus" tip and Part 13's "Opus 4.8, strongest yet." When you pick a model for coding, Fable 5 now leads. "Less prompts and steers" → lean into minimalism + delegation That's exactly the world Part 15's context minimalism and Part 10's delegation-over-guidance describe - give it the goal, not the micro-steps. Longer sessions + higher autonomy → the autonomy stack pays off more Auto mode (Parts 8, 11), /goal (Part 12), nested subagents (Part 16), and workflows (Parts 13-14) all benefit from a base model that self-verifies better and needs less babysitting. Caveat Pricing is live - $10/M input · $50/M output , exactly 2× Opus 4.8's $5/$25. Model id claude-fable-5 ; 1M context, 128K max output, adaptive thinking, knowledge cutoff Jan 2026; no fast mode yet. Fable-specific effort levels and usage best-practices aren't documented yet. ← fable 5 back to intro →

blocks.heading: Finding Your Unknowns - The Map Is Not the Territory
blocks.text: Finding Your Unknowns - The Map Is Not the Territory Thariq (@trq212, Claude Code) says working with Fable 5 keeps re-teaching one lesson: "the map is not the territory." The map is what you give Claude - your prompts, skills, and context. The territory is where the work actually happens - the codebase, the real world, its actual constraints. The gap between them is what he calls your unknowns . Fable is the first model where he finds the quality of the work is bottlenecked by his ability to clarify those unknowns - so "reducing and planning for your unknowns is the skill of agentic coding." The good news: it's a skill you can improve at, by working with Claude. @trq212 · July 3, 2026 Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: The Four Unknowns
blocks.text: 1 The Four Unknowns When Thariq brings a problem to Claude, he breaks it down four ways - the Rumsfeld matrix, applied to prompting: ▤ Known knowns what's in your prompt What you tell the agent you want. ? Known unknowns questions you know to ask What you haven't figured out yet, but you're aware you haven't. ◉ Unknown knowns "I'll know it when I see it" What's so obvious you'd never write it down, but you'd recognize it if you saw it. ⚠ Unknown unknowns what you never considered The pothole you didn't know the road could have. The more work being done, the more of these Claude will run into. When Claude hits an unknown, it has to make a decision based on its best guess of what you want. "The best agentic coders have relatively few unknowns," Thariq writes - watching someone like Boris or Jarred prompt, it's obvious they know what they want in detail and are deeply in-sync with both the codebase and the model's behaviors. But they also assume unknowns. Reducing and planning for them is the actual skill of agentic coding - and the rest of this Part is his toolkit for finding them before, during, and after implementation. ← intro before →

blocks.heading: Before Implementation
blocks.text: 2 Before Implementation Most unknowns are cheapest to find before you write code. Thariq's pre-implementation techniques, each with the literal prompts he uses: Blind spot pass Ask Claude to find your unknown unknowns and explain them - he uses the literal words "blindspot pass." Give it context on who you are and what you already know. I'm working on adding a new auth provider but I know nothing about the auth modules in this codebase. Can you do a blindspot pass to help me figure out my relevant unknown unknowns and help me prompt you better. Brainstorms & prototypes - for unknown knowns When the criteria are ones you'll only recognize when you see them (visual design, layout), ask Claude to brainstorm and prototype. An HTML artifact you can react to beats trying to describe it. I want a dashboard for this data but I have no visual taste and don't know what's possible. Make me an HTML page with 4 wildly different design directions so I can react to them. Interviews Once you've brainstormed, ask Claude to interview you about remaining ambiguities - one question at a time, prioritizing questions whose answer would change the architecture. Interview me one question at a time about anything ambiguous, prioritize questions where my answer would change the architecture. References - the best reference is source code When you can't describe what you want, point Claude at a reference. Diagrams and pictures work, but the best reference is source code - point Fable at a folder or a module on a website and it reads the underlying code, not just the screenshot. This is also how Claude Design works: richer detail on markup, structure, and how the thing is actually built. Implementation plans Ask for a plan that leads with the parts most likely to change - data models, type interfaces, UX flows - so Claude surfaces what you might actually need to alter, and buries the mechanical refactoring. Write an implementation plan in HTML, but lead with the decisions I'm most likely to tweak: data model changes, new type interfaces, and anything user-facing. Bury the mechanical refactoring at the bottom, I trust you on that part. ← 4 unknowns during →

blocks.heading: During Implementation
blocks.text: 3 During Implementation No matter how much you plan, there are always unknown unknowns lurking - the agent may hit an edge case mid-work that forces a different tack. Implementation notes Ask Claude Code to keep a temporary implementation-notes.md (or .html ) file where it logs the decisions it makes, so you can learn from them on the next attempt. Keep an implementation-notes.md file. If you hit an edge case that forces you to deviate from the plan, pick the conservative option, log it under 'Deviations', and keep going. This pairs with Part 15's "write it down" discipline - what the agent learns mid-run becomes the map for next time, instead of evaporating when the session ends. ← before after →

blocks.heading: After Implementation
blocks.text: 4 After Implementation Once the work lands, the remaining unknowns are other people's - your reviewers' and your own future understanding. Pitches & explainers Getting buy-in is one of the most important parts of shipping. Package the prototype, the spec, and the implementation notes into a single doc you can drop in Slack - lead with the demo. Reviewers start with the same unknowns you did, so answer them up front. Package the prototype, the spec, and the implementation notes into a single doc I can drop in Slack to get buy-in. Lead with the demo GIF. Quizzes - merge only when you pass After a long session Claude may have done more than you realized, and reading diffs only gives a light understanding. Ask Claude to quiz you about the change after giving you context - Thariq only merges after passing the quiz perfectly. Give me an HTML report on the changes to read and understand with context, intuition, and what was done - and a quiz at the bottom on the changes that I must pass. How it comes together: launching Fable The Fable launch video was edited entirely by Claude Code - a domain Thariq was "by no means an expert" in. He ran exactly this loop: started from what he knew (Claude can edit and transcribe video), asked Claude to explain how transcription and ffmpeg cutting worked, prototyped a timed UI with Remotion, and - realizing he didn't know what "good" color grading looked like - asked Claude to teach him his unknowns rather than guess at variations. "The better models get, the more you can achieve with the right approach... So start your next project by asking Claude to help you find your unknowns." ← during back to intro →

blocks.heading: Getting Started With Loops
blocks.text: Getting Started With Loops The Claude Code team defines a loop as an agent repeating cycles of work until a stop condition is met . Everything from a single prompt to a cloud routine is a loop - they differ only in how they're triggered , how they're stopped , which Claude Code primitive runs them, and what kind of task fits. This guide maps the four types and when to reach for each. Not every task needs a complex loop - start with the simplest one and use these patterns selectively. @ClaudeDevs · July 6, 2026 Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: The Four Loops
blocks.text: 1 The Four Loops Every loop in Claude Code fits one of four shapes. They differ by what triggers them, what stops them, and - most usefully - how much of the loop you hand off: ↻ Turn-based the agentic loop Triggered by a prompt; stops when Claude judges the task done. Best for shorter, one-off tasks. You hand off the check . ◎ Goal-based · /goal until the condition is met Triggered by a prompt; stops when the goal is met or a turn cap is hit. Best when you have verifiable exit criteria. You hand off the stop condition . ⏱ Time-based · /loop · /schedule on an interval Triggered by a time interval; stops when you cancel or the work completes. Best for recurring work or reacting to external systems. You hand off the trigger . ⚡ Proactive event-driven, no human Triggered by an event or schedule with no human in real time; each task exits at its goal, the routine runs until you turn it off. Best for recurring streams of well-defined work. You hand off the prompt . Notice the progression: moving from turn-based to proactive, you hand off more of the loop each step - first the verification check, then the stop condition, then the trigger, and finally the prompt itself. Tab 4 has the full "which loop when" table. ← intro you drive →

blocks.heading: Loops You Drive - Turn-based & Goal-based
blocks.text: 2 Loops You Drive - Turn-based & Goal-based The two real-time loops: you kick them off and stay close. Turn-based - the agentic loop Every prompt you send is already a loop: Claude gathers context, takes action, checks its work, repeats if needed, and responds - exiting when it judges the task complete or the effort budget runs out. The lever is verification: encode your manual check steps as a SKILL.md so Claude verifies its own work end-to-end, and give it tools to see, measure, interact (the more quantitative the check, the easier it self-verifies). Builds on verification and Part 18's verification skills . Create a verify-frontend-change skill: never call a UI change done from a successful edit alone. Start the dev server, open the page, interact with the change, confirm zero new console errors, and run a Chrome DevTools MCP performance trace. If any step fails, fix it and rerun from the top. Goal-based - /goal A single turn often isn't enough, and agents do better when they can iterate. /goal lets you define what "done" looks like so Claude can't quietly decide it's "good enough" and stop early. Each time it tries to stop, an evaluator model checks your condition and sends it back to work until the goal is met or your turn cap is reached. Deterministic criteria - tests passing, a score threshold - work best. Extends /goal (see Part 12). /goal get the homepage Lighthouse score to 90 or above, stop after 5 tries ← the four loops runs without you →

blocks.heading: Loops That Run Without You - Time-based & Proactive
blocks.text: 3 Loops That Run Without You - Time-based & Proactive The two autonomous loops: the work comes to Claude instead of you prompting each time. Time-based - /loop and /schedule For work that's recurring (same task, changing inputs - a morning Slack summary) or that reacts to an external system (a PR that gets reviews or fails CI). /loop re-runs a prompt on an interval on your machine - turn your laptop off and it stops. Move it to the cloud by turning it into a Routine with /schedule . Pulls together /loop , /schedule , and Routines . /loop 5m check my PR, address review comments, and fix failing CI Proactive - compose the whole stack The most autonomous loop: triggered by an event or schedule with no human in real time, running in the cloud whether your laptop is open or not. You compose the primitives - /schedule to watch for new work, /goal + verification skills to define and check "done," dynamic workflows to orchestrate triage/fix/review across many items, and auto mode so it never stops to ask permission. Each task exits at its goal; the routine runs until you turn it off. /schedule every hour: check the project-feedback channel for bug reports, triage each one, open a PR with a fix, and have a second agent review it before notifying me ← you drive make them good →

blocks.heading: Making Loops Good - Quality, Tokens & Which One When
blocks.text: 4 Making Loops Good - Quality, Tokens & Which One When A loop is only as good as the system around it. Two things to get right, plus a cheat sheet. Keep the output quality high Keep the codebase clean - Claude follows the patterns already there. Give it a way to verify its own work - encode what "good" looks like as skills. Make docs easy to reach - framework and library docs carry current best practices. Use a second agent for review - fresh context is less biased; the built-in /code-review or Code Review for GitHub. When a result misses the bar, don't just fix the instance - encode the fix so every future iteration improves. Manage token usage Right primitive + model - small tasks don't need a fleet; use cheaper/faster models for routine work. Clear stop criteria - specific "done" so Claude lands sooner (but not too soon). Pilot before a large run - dynamic workflows can spawn hundreds of agents; gauge on a slice first. Scripts for deterministic work - running a script beats re-reasoning the steps each time. Don't over-schedule - match the interval to how often the thing you watch actually changes. Review usage - /usage breaks down skills/subagents/MCPs; /goal with no args shows turns + tokens so far; /workflows shows per-agent usage and lets you stop one. Which loop when Loop You hand off Use it when Reach for Turn-based The check You're exploring or deciding Custom verification skills Goal-based The stop condition You know what done looks like /goal Time-based The trigger The work happens on a schedule, outside your project /loop , /schedule Proactive The prompt The work is recurring and well-defined All of the above + dynamic workflows To get started, look at the work you already do, pick one task where you're the bottleneck, and ask which piece you could hand off - the verification check, the stop condition, or the trigger. Run the loop, watch where it stalls or over-reaches, and iterate. ← runs without you back to intro →

blocks.heading: Give Your Setup a /checkup
blocks.text: Give Your Setup a /checkup Every setup drifts - skills you stopped using, a CLAUDE.md that quietly grew to 10k tokens, hooks that slow every turn, a version that's three releases behind. Boris shipped /checkup : one command that audits your whole Claude Code install, tells you exactly what's wasteful or broken, and cleans it up - after it confirms with you, and always reversibly. It's the whole "keep your setup lean" playbook - context minimalism, CLAUDE.md hygiene, writing fixes down instead of re-prompting - turned into a single command. @bcherny · July 8, 2026 Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: /checkup - The One-Command Tune-Up
blocks.text: 1 /checkup - The One-Command Tune-Up Run /checkup and Claude Code inspects your setup for waste, staleness, and breakage, then proposes fixes across seven areas: What /checkup cleans up Clean up unused skills / MCPs / plugins - drop what you never invoke and save context every session ( context minimalism ). Dedup your local CLAUDE.md against the checked-in one so rules aren't stated twice. Break up a big root CLAUDE.md into nested CLAUDE.md's + skills, so context loads only where it's relevant. Turn off slow hooks that tax every turn. Update Claude Code to the latest version. Enable auto mode by default so it stops asking permission for safe work. Pre-approve frequently-denied read-only commands - the same idea as /fewer-permission-prompts . ...and a few other goodies. Think of it as a periodic tune-up: the hygiene tips scattered across this catalog, run for you in one pass. /checkup ← intro safe by default →

blocks.heading: Safe by Default - Confirms First, Fully Reversible
blocks.text: 2 Safe by Default - Confirms First, Fully Reversible The reason you can run /checkup on a real project without holding your breath: it never changes anything behind your back. It confirms before it touches anything /checkup surfaces a plan first - here's what's broken, here's what's unused, here's what it'd change - and waits for your call. Nothing is modified until you pick an option. Everything is reversible Settings changes are one-line toggles you can flip back. CLAUDE.md edits stay in your working tree, so you review them in git diff before you commit a thing - same discipline as writing fixes down instead of re-prompting. You're always in control of scope Clean up everything - the recommended one-shot. Let me pick - choose which groups to touch (install repair, unused plugins/MCP, unused skills, CLAUDE.md slimming). No, keep everything - report only; nothing changes. Chat about this - ask questions before deciding. ← /checkup the run →

blocks.heading: The Run - What It Actually Found
blocks.text: 3 The Run - What It Actually Found Boris ran /checkup on his own setup and posted the result. It caught things he didn't know were there: The findings His claude command was broken - a test run had overwritten its launcher. 38 project skills had never been used across 2,345 sessions . His CLAUDE.md was loading ~10k tokens every session . Cleaning it all up repairs the install and saves roughly 5.5k tokens of context per session - a permanent tax lifted off every future turn. The recommended fix (one keystroke) Repair the broken launcher, disable 3 unused plugins + the hex MCP server + 1 stray skill, turn off the 38 never-used project skills, and slim CLAUDE.md by moving ~1.9k tokens of content to lazy loading. Reversible, as always - the CLAUDE.md edits land in your working tree for git diff review. The lesson underneath the feature: setups accumulate silent waste, and you rarely notice until something measures it. /checkup is that measurement - the maintenance half of context minimalism, automated. ← safe by default back to intro →

blocks.heading: Automation Is the Meta-Skill
blocks.text: Automation Is the Meta-Skill The best engineers always spent their time automating - vim macros, lint rules, e2e suites - because it multiplied their own output. Boris argues that in the agent era this matters more , for three reasons: it speeds up your whole fleet, it moves fixes into code so a class of bug is gone forever, and - most importantly - it lets anyone contribute by encoding domain knowledge as infrastructure instead of leaving it stuck in people's heads. The punchline: a rejected PR is a failure of automation. @bcherny · July 15, 2026 Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: Automation Is the Highest-Leverage Work
blocks.text: 1 Automation Is the Highest-Leverage Work The through-line hasn't changed - only gotten stronger. The best engineers Boris knew always poured time into automating their own work, because it multiplied everything else they did. Old world, sharpened Better vim/emacs macros, lint rules that catch a repeat issue automatically, an e2e suite so you never smoke-test by hand - these were the highest-leverage activities an engineer could do, because they multiplied their own output. That logic didn't go away with agents; it compounded. Infra and DevX automation speeds you up - and if you're running an army of agents, every one of them is sped up too. So the payoff stopped being linear: more automation = more output per unit of time × your number of agents Pairs with parallel execution (Part 1) and loops (Part 19). ← intro fixes into code →

blocks.heading: Move Fixes From Prompts Into Code
blocks.text: 2 Move Fixes From Prompts Into Code There's a difference between fixing an issue and eliminating a class of issue. The first is a chat correction; the second is infrastructure. One-off fix The agent fixes the issue every time it sees it - spends tokens on every run, and might miss cases. ▸ Encoded rule Claude writes a lint rule, CI step, or routine - the whole class is caught automatically, forever, for every contributor. Boris: this is "really what people are talking about when they talk about loops - it's about automating entire types of busywork rather than solving them one off." Not a new idea - engineers have done it for a long time - but agents make it cheap to reach for. It generalizes write it down, don't re-prompt (Part 15): a chat correction fixes one run; encoded infrastructure fixes every run (Part 19). ← highest leverage knowledge as infra →

blocks.heading: Encode Domain Knowledge as Infrastructure
blocks.text: 3 Encode Domain Knowledge as Infrastructure The most important reason, and the one that's genuinely new. Automation is what lets other people - not just you - contribute to a codebase. What used to block contribution Engineers now contribute on day one because Claude can navigate the codebase for them, and non-engineers can contribute as effectively as engineers. What gets in the way of both is domain knowledge that lives in people's heads - the stuff you used to have to learn while ramping up. What's changed: the knowledge you can encode as infrastructure is no longer limited to lint rules, types, and tests. It can now capture nearly all domain knowledge - code comments skills CLAUDE.md REVIEW.md docs memories - so an agent (or a new human) works productively with zero additional context from the prompter . Builds directly on CLAUDE.md (Part 1), skills (Part 2), and code review (Part 6). If I put up a PR for an iOS codebase I don't know and a reviewer rejects it because it doesn't use the right framework, or a designer's feature gets rejected because it doesn't follow the right architectural patterns - these are failures of automation. - Boris Cherny. The knowledge should have been in the infra, not a reviewer's head. Every team should be writing the CLAUDE.md's, REVIEW.md's, skills, and docs that let agents work in their codebase with zero extra context. It sounds extreme, but it's the natural extension of what engineers have always done: automate, and encode domain knowledge as infrastructure - so Claude writes better code, review catches issues automatically, and the next person contributes more easily. ← fixes into code back to intro →

blocks.heading: The New Rules of Context Engineering
blocks.text: The New Rules of Context Engineering Your prompt is only a sliver of what Claude actually reads - the rest is assembled from the system prompt, CLAUDE.md, skills, memory, and references. That's context engineering , and the rules just changed. Tuning Claude Code for the Claude 5 generation, the team deleted over 80% of the system prompt with no measurable loss on coding evals. Thariq distilled what they learned into six then→now shifts, and every one says the same thing: stop over-constraining the model and let its judgement do the work. It lands the same day as Opus 5 - the model these rules are written for. @trq212 · July 24, 2026 Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: Give Judgement, Not Rules
blocks.text: 1 Give Judgement, Not Rules The headline shift. Older models needed rigid guardrails to avoid worst-case behavior - but a rule that's right 90% of the time is wrong the other 10%. Newer models read the surrounding context and decide for themselves, so the team swapped hard rules for judgement. The system prompt's comment guidance is the cleanest example: Then - a rule "In code: default to writing no comments. Never write multi-paragraph docstrings or multi-line comment blocks - one short line max." ▸ Now - judgement "Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom." The rule was wrong everywhere comments were wanted - documentation, gnarly code. Judgement handles both cases without a special rule for each. That's how they cut the prompt so hard: -80% of Claude Code's system prompt removed for Opus 5 / Fable 5 = no measurable eval loss The mirror worth holding up: most CLAUDE.md files (this repo's included) are still walls of hard rules and banned phrases. Updates context minimalism (Part 15). ← intro design interfaces →

blocks.heading: Design Interfaces, Not Examples
blocks.text: 2 Design Interfaces, Not Examples The old number-one rule for tools was to give Claude worked examples. With the newest models, examples backfire - they fence Claude into the exploration space you happened to demonstrate. Design the interface instead, and let expressive parameters do the teaching. TodoWrite, without a single example The tool ships no walkthrough. Its shape teaches usage: a status parameter that can only be one of three values, plus one constraint on how they move. pending in_progress completed only one in_progress at a time The enum hints at the lifecycle; the "one in_progress" rule pins down the behavior - no example needed. Ask the same of your own tools, scripts, and files: what parameters does Claude have, and how could they be more expressive ? A rich interface beats a page of examples. (Same idea for design: an HTML mockup beats a described layout or a screenshot - see tab 4.) ← judgement progressive disclosure →

blocks.heading: Progressive Disclosure Over Front-Loading
blocks.text: 3 Progressive Disclosure Over Front-Loading Don't cram everything a request might need into the prompt. Load context at the moment it's relevant - the same principle whether it's the built-in system prompt, tools, or your own files. Surface Then - all upfront Now - loaded when needed System prompt Code-review & verification steps baked in Moved into skills Claude calls selectively Tools Every definition always in context Deferred loading - searched via ToolSearch before use CLAUDE.md / skills One mega-file with every practice A tree of files loaded at the right time The myth is that CLAUDE.md and skills should be a central repository for everything you might hit, because Claude won't find it otherwise. It will. Split long skills across many files and let Claude pull the branch it needs. And stop repeating yourself Older models leaned on repetition and end-of-context reminders, so instructions got duplicated in both the system prompt and the tool description. Newer models don't need it - put tool instructions in the tool description only , and delete the echo. ← interfaces memory & references →

blocks.heading: Auto-Memory & Rich References
blocks.text: 4 Auto-Memory & Rich References Two shifts in how Claude remembers, and what you point it at. Memory in CLAUDE.md → Auto-memory You used to hand-save context to CLAUDE.md with the # hotkey. Now Claude automatically saves memories relevant to the work and to you, and loads them across sessions - memory, artifacts, and skills take over the job CLAUDE.md used to do alone. Builds on auto-memory (Part 8) and write-it-down (Part 15). And references got richer. A "spec" no longer means a markdown file - Claude handles far more expressive references, and code-shaped ones carry the highest fidelity: ▦ HTML artifacts A working mockup from the artifacts feature - a real design beats a screenshot or a description. </> Code as spec A function in another codebase to port - an instruction in a language Claude already knows cold. ✓ Test suites A detailed suite is a spec that verifies itself. ★ Rubrics Encode your taste - what good API design looks like - and verifier agents in a dynamic workflow check against it. ← progressive disclosure your context →

blocks.heading: Applying It to Your Own Context
blocks.text: 5 Applying It to Your Own Context Pull it together - here's the stack Claude assembles for a request, top to bottom, and what belongs in each layer: The assembled context Your prompt - the one specific thing you want right now. References - @-mentioned files, specs, mockups, codebases, artifacts. System prompt - tied to the product; you rarely touch it in Claude Code (spend real time here only if you're building your own agent). CLAUDE.md - lightweight: what the repo is for, and the gotchas . Skip the obvious; push detail into skills via progressive disclosure. Skills - lightweight guides for your opinions and best practices; avoid over-constraining except in high-stakes areas. Memory - now automatic. Can't tell what to cut? Run /doctor The new claude doctor command ( /doctor in Claude Code) rightsizes your skills and CLAUDE.md automatically - the context-engineering twin of Part 20's /checkup . /doctor ← memory & references opus 5 →

blocks.heading: Opus 5 - And the Model That's Hardest to Inject
blocks.text: 6 Opus 5 - And the Model That's Hardest to Inject These rules ship for a reason. Opus 5 landed the same day - state-of-the-art on coding and knowledge-work evals (agentic terminal coding, GDPval, ARC-AGI-3, computer use). But the eval scores aren't what Boris led with. The least prompt-injectable model yet Across prompt-injection evals and red-teaming, Opus 5 is very hard to inject. Layer the defenses - strong model alignment, prompt-injection probes, and Auto Mode in Claude Code - and the attack success rate collapses. prompt-injection attacks vs. Opus 5 + PI probes + auto mode success rate → ~0% That's the ground the new rules stand on: judgement-based context engineering only works if you can trust the model to reconcile conflicting, attacker-adjacent context safely. Pairs with why auto mode is trustworthy (Part 15). More than any of these eval scores, what is most exciting to me is something else: Opus 5 is our least prompt injectable model yet. - Boris Cherny, on the Opus 5 launch ← your context back to intro →

parts.title: The New Rules of Context Engineering

blocks.heading: Claude Maintains the Apps
blocks.text: Claude Maintains the Apps Part 21 argued that moving fixes out of prompts and into routines is the highest-leverage thing an engineer can do. This is the receipt. For a few weeks Boris has had Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of Anthropic's apps - a Slack channel, a dozen daily routines, and no one driving. The result: 388 PRs opened, 180 merged across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and the Agent SDK. The interesting part isn't that it works. It's the specific list of jobs worth handing over, and the operating habits that keep the output mergeable. @bcherny · August 13, 2026 Click the tabs above to explore each tip → or use ← → arrow keys

blocks.heading: What to Actually Automate
blocks.text: 1 What to Actually Automate Every guide tells you to set up routines. Almost none tell you what to point them at. Boris published his list - the daily jobs running against Anthropic's own apps - and it's the most concrete answer anyone has given: Routine What it does Crash fuzzer Finds real-app crashes and opens root-cause fixes Ant-only shipper Ships or deletes forgotten internal-only features based on usage Logic simplifier Simplifies convoluted business logic Logic bugfixer Models tricky logic to find and fix bugs Dup unifier Merges duplicated implementations into one Dead-code removal Deletes provably unreachable code Useless-test pruner Deletes tests that can't fail Shipped-feature inliner Removes flags for fully shipped features Flaky-test fixer Root-causes flaky CI tests Abstraction improver Flattens over-engineered abstractions Abstraction police Fixes layering violations Notice what they have in common: every one is mechanical, verifiable, and endless - the maintenance you keep meaning to get to. None of them are feature work. Each runs as a separate routine per app, across every surface: iOS Android Desktop web CLI Agent SDK Output lands in one Slack channel, proj-claude-maintains-apps , with a top-level thread per routine so a dozen parallel jobs stay readable. Picks up where Part 10 (Routines) and Part 21 (automation as infrastructure) left off. ← intro probe, then delete →

blocks.heading: Probe, Then Delete
blocks.text: 2 Probe, Then Delete The dead-code routine is the cleverest thing in the thread, and it's easy to miss. Static analysis only proves the easy half - code nothing references. The code that's reachable but never actually runs is the stuff that accumulates for years, and no analyzer can tell you it's safe to cut. So the routine doesn't guess. It splits the job across two days. The obvious routine Delete what looks unreachable. Anything merely suspected dead stays forever, because nobody will risk it. ▸ What Boris runs Delete what's provably unreachable. For the rest, add logging , wait a day, and remove whatever never fired. Day one gathers evidence; day two acts on it. That's a shape worth stealing beyond dead code - any time a routine needs a fact it can't derive from a static read, have it instrument the codebase and read its own results on the next run. A routine that runs daily can afford to be patient. The whole thing was requested in eight words: also do one for dead code removal The two-phase design wasn't specified. Claude worked out that a probe was needed - which is what Part 22's "give judgement, not rules" looks like in production. ← what to automate truth tables →

blocks.heading: Make the Routine Prove It
blocks.text: 3 Make the Routine Prove It An autonomous routine opening PRs all day is only useful if reviewing each one is cheap. Boris solved that by demanding evidence in the prompt itself - every PR arrives carrying its own proof: each pr must run /verify and post a repro and truth table to the pr And for the logic routines, the bar goes further - model the behavior formally before touching it: From the routine prompt "always verify e2e with truth table. for all of these, remember to formally model the logic also to spot gaps and duplication and to make sure all edge cases are well tested" A truth table turns "trust me, this refactor is equivalent" into something a reviewer checks in seconds. It also does quiet double duty: enumerating the cases is how the routine finds the gaps and duplication it's supposed to fix. The verification artifact and the discovery method are the same work. Also in the prompt: run the real apps, no mocks . A crash fuzzer against a mock finds mock bugs. Extends the verification-as-a-skill idea from Part 19. ← probe, then delete tune the routine →

blocks.heading: Tune the Routine, Not the PR
blocks.text: 4 Tune the Routine, Not the PR The habit that makes the whole system compound. When a PR comes back wrong, the instinct is to fix the PR. Boris fixes the routine instead, and lets tomorrow's run produce a better PR on its own. fix the PR = one better PR · fix the routine = every future PR The corollary is a patience most people don't budget for. A routine isn't right on day one, and that's not a failure signal: Claude generally gets these PRs right on the first shot, and if it doesn't, we ask Claude to tune its routines so it's better the next day. Sometimes it takes a few days of tuning. - Boris Cherny Note who does the tuning. He doesn't rewrite the prompt himself - he asks Claude to tune its own routine. The routine is the artifact under development, and the daily cadence is its feedback loop. Judge a routine on its trend across a week, not its first PR. ← truth tables the yield →

blocks.heading: Expect Half to Land
blocks.text: 5 Expect Half to Land The number worth carrying around, because it sets expectations honestly. Over a few weeks of daily routines across six surfaces: 388 PRs opened → 180 merged = 46% Not 95%, and not 10%. Roughly half of autonomous maintenance work is good enough to keep - which is an excellent return on code nobody was going to write, and a terrible return if you were planning to merge on trust. Nothing lands unreviewed: Two gates, both kept Every PR passes Claude Code Review first, then human review . The automation generates the work; it doesn't approve it. Which locates the real bottleneck. With generation nearly free, the constraint moves to review throughput - and that's exactly where Boris says the work is heading next: "We're now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier." The routines aren't the hard part anymore. Merging is. To try it: ask Claude Code or Tag to set one up, or create routines directly at claude.ai/code/routines . Start with one routine on one repo - the eleven above took weeks of tuning to reach 46%. ← tune the routine back to intro →
